newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTZ-CRA sells Australian zinc deposit amid land row.
newsitem.headline: RTZ-CRA sells Australian zinc deposit amid land row.

text.p: Global mining titan RTZ-CRA announced on Thursday it was selling its vast Century zinc deposit, beset by land claims from Australian Aborigines, to local miner Pasminco Ltd for A$345 million (US$269 million).
RTZ-CRA denied it was walking away from the A$1 billion project out of frustration at Australia's changing approach to Aborginal land claims.

"It's a commercial deal and in no way does it reflect frustration or throwing our hands in the air over the native title issue," CRA Ltd managing director Leigh Clifford told a news briefing in Melbourne.

"A$345 million for the two assets is a very good return for us ... and it's better than what we thought was achievable," Clifford said, adding that a smaller zinc deposit nearby was also included in the sale.
Pasminco has made a downpayment of A$10 million but the balance is payable only if protracted talks between Century Zinc management and local Aborigines conclude with the granting of valid leases.
Australian mining analysts welcomed the deal which Pasminco said trebles its zinc resources, securing its position as the world's largest zinc producer.
"It's good for Pasminco and a decisive decision from RTZ-CRA ... the major benefit (for Pasminco) is it now has a long-life ore body," said CS First Boston director of minerals Ray Chantry.

CRA, part of a dual-listed entity with London-based mining giant RTZ Corp Plc, discovered the magnitude of the Century deposit in northwest Queensland state in 1990 and planned to develop a mine producing 780,000 tonnes of mainly zinc concentrate a year.
It contracted Pasminco, the world's biggest lead and zinc producer, to take about half of the mine's output from mid-1998.

Pasminco, which badly needs Century's low-iron zinc supplies to comply with a planned environmental crackdown on its big Budel zinc smelter in the Netherlands, approached RTZ-CRA about purchasing the deposit last year, the parties said on Thursday.

RTZ-CRA was at the time in the eye of a political storm over indigenous land claims and protests from miners and some conservative state governments that claims for so-called native title were bogging down resource developments.

RTZ-CRA and Aboriginal leaders began negotiations outside official channels in earnest in 1995, but after failing to strike a deal, the firm opted last July to continue talks under the controversial native title process.
Australia's Labor government in 1993 passed legislation allowing Aborigines to claim land if they could prove uninterrupted traditional use of that land.
"Negotiations are proceeding and I would not want to preempt those discussions, but I think they are proceeding satisfactorily," Clifford told reporters on Thursday.
Pasminco managing director David Stewart said that under the nation's Native Title Act, a settlement must be reached by September.
Pasminco shares dipped six cents to A$1.92 after the sale announcement, with some investors apparently worried by the company's plan to equity-fund part of Century's developent.

"They've confirmed that to fund (the mine development) there would be a mix of equity and debt, so that was probably the concern that...drove the share price down," said HSBC James Capel institutional dealer David Iron.
But he added the share price's longer term future was seen more closely allied to zinc prices.
"If zinc was to improve significantly in price and the transaction was finally consummated, people might not mind providing new equity to Pasminco."
